references.text: The psalmist says that God satisfies the hungry soul, which corresponds to the promise that those who hunger now will be filled.
Those who sow with tears shall reap with joy – the same contrast between present weeping and future joy as in Luke 6:21b.
Isaiah invites those who hunger and thirst to come and be satisfied, a prophetic promise underlying Jesus’ beatitude of the hungry.

The Messiah is anointed to proclaim good news to the poor and comfort all who mourn, so that they may receive the oil of gladness instead of sorrow – the background for the promise that those who weep will laugh.
The Lord says that his servants shall eat and rejoice, while those who forsake him shall hunger and weep – a contrast between the righteousness’ fullness and joy and the wicked’s hunger and sorrow.
The Lord promises to satisfy the weary soul and fill every longing soul, a promise of satisfaction for those who hunger.
In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus says: Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted – a parallel beatitude to the promise that those who weep now will laugh.
Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled – Matthew’s parallel to Luke’s beatitude of the hungry.
Jesus says that whoever comes to him shall not hunger, and whoever believes in him shall never thirst – the fulfillment of the promise of satisfaction.

James urges people to mourn and weep, letting laughter turn to sorrow – but with the promise that whoever humbles themselves before the Lord will be exalted, in line with the turning of weeping into joy.
In the final consummation they shall no longer hunger or thirst, and God shall wipe away every tear – the eschatological fulfillment of the promise in Luke 6:21.
God shall wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, nor sorrow or weeping – the ultimate fulfillment of the promise to those who weep now.
